Each type has its own unique characteristics and uses, but they all serve to organize and store data in a way that makes it easy to access, manipulate, and understand. 1. Arrays: A collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations. They are accessed using an index number. 2. Linked Lists: A linear collection of data elements, called nodes, which contain a data field and a reference (link) to the next node in the sequence. They are useful for dynamic size and efficient insertion/deletion. 3. Stacks: A last-in, first-out (LIFO) data structure that stores elements in a single list in a manner such that the last element added is the first one to be removed. They are used for functions calls and undo operations. 4. Queues: A first-in, first-out (FIFO) data structure that stores elements in two separate lists: one for the front of the queue and one for the back. They are useful for scheduling tasks and simulating real-world systems like a line at a bank or a printing system. 5. Trees: A hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes where each node has zero
